entities.name: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, opened 1955 in Hiroshima, Japan, adjacent to the Hiroshima Peace Memorial (Genbaku Dome — the only surviving structure near the bomb's hypocenter, preserved at 160 meters from ground zero), documents the August 6, 1945 atomic bombing that killed 70,000-80,000 people instantly and 90,000-140,000 within four months — the first use of nuclear weapons in war — through survivor testimony, personal artifacts, and graphic documentation that made it the global center of nuclear abolition advocacy. The museum's visitors include every US President who has visited Japan.

The atomic bomb 'Little Boy' (uranium gun-type device, 15 kiloton yield) exploded 580 meters above Hiroshima at 8:15 AM on August 6, 1945. The hypocenter was 160 meters southeast of the Genbaku Dome (Hiroshima Prefectural Industrial Promotion Hall). The dome's iron skeleton survived because the blast was almost directly overhead; it was preserved as a memorial and designated UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996. The museum's founding in 1955 was an act of deliberate memory against nuclear forgetting.

The museum's exhibits include a child's destroyed tricycle, a shadow burned into stone steps (where a human body vaporized, leaving only a shadow), watch faces stopped at 8:15, and vivid survivor (hibakusha) testimonies. President Obama became the first sitting US president to visit in May 2016 — a visit watched worldwide, though he did not apologize for the bombing. Over 1.7 million visitors annually include school groups from across Japan as part of mandatory peace education.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum — preserving the human reality of the first nuclear weapon use in war through survivor artifacts and testimony — has been the world's most powerful argument for nuclear abolition for 70 years, making it the museum whose collection could most directly save human lives if heeded.
